requirements.requirement: Publish node2's TCP/8080 application through node1 so node3 can reach it
requirements.summary: Ansible-applied VyOS destination NAT (PREROUTING: iifname eth0 tcp dport 8080 dnat to 10.50.50.2:8080) was verified live in nftables, and node3's curl to node1's mgmt address (10.100.88.10:8080) returned the expected app response 'hello from node2 app on port 8080' both immediately after configuration and again after all four nodes were rebooted.

requirements.requirement: Do not open the rest of the private lan network to node3
requirements.summary: The forward filter shows only an established/related accept rule and a narrow DNAT-flow accept rule (dest 10.50.50.2 tcp/8080 in-iface eth0), with a default-drop catch-all. Direct node3 attempts to reach node2's private address (10.50.50.2:8080) were refused ('Host is unreachable') both pre- and post-reboot, confirming no broader lan exposure.

An ansible-playbook run from the designated control node (node4) against a vyos/appserver/verifier inventory performed the eth1 addressing, NAT/firewall configuration, application service setup, and end-to-end verification assertions, completing with a clean PLAY RECAP (zero failed) both initially and after all nodes rebooted.

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes were all satisfied: node1's VyOS destination-NAT and default-drop forward filter publish node2's port-8080 app to node3 while keeping the rest of the private lan closed, implemented and verified through an Ansible playbook run from the control node. End-to-end reachability and isolation were directly confirmed via node3 curl/nc probes both before and after a full round of node reboots across all four managed nodes, with boot-identity changes and recovered NAT/firewall/service/route state observed on each. Hygiene is moderately good but not clean: a root-SSH sshd_config edit on node1 was abandoned mid-troubleshooting and left unreverted, and PermitRootLogin was set more permissively ('yes') than necessary on the Alpine nodes.
limitations: The mandatory provider-wide restart protocol was carried out on all four nodes with matching pre/post boot-identity, service, and connectivity evidence, but this is a supplemental protocol independent of the public task contract and does not itself count toward satisfying the port-forwarding requirements.

The abandoned sshd_config edit on node1 (PermitRootLogin yes) was never confirmed reverted or applied, since the subsequent restart attempt failed and the executor switched to the working vyos-user/pubkey path instead — its final effective state on node1 could not be independently confirmed from the given evidence.

Command outputs are bounded/truncated in places (e.g., long ansible-playbook runs), so some intermediate task-level detail (exact task names/counts) is inferred from summarized recap lines rather than full raw output.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state changes (eth1 addressing, NAT/firewall rules, webapp service, host route, python3 bootstrap) were necessary prerequisites executed via Ansible and left in a working, idempotent state. However several unnecessary or oversized mutations occurred: (1) on node1 the executor edited /etc/ssh/sshd_config to 'PermitRootLogin yes' and attempted a systemctl restart that failed (bind conflict with the socket-activated ssh@default.service) — this was an abandoned troubleshooting path since the final solution authenticates to node1 as the 'vyos' user via VyOS's own login config, not root SSH, and the sshd_config edit was never confirmed reverted (cmd-f85a28d3a3a24ce6, cmd-17444a85f5ce4703). (2) On node2 and node3 the executor set PermitRootLogin to the broader 'yes' (allowing root password auth) rather than restoring the original 'prohibit-password' default, which already permits pubkey-based root login once the account is unlocked — a modest, retained weakening of a security control beyond what was needed (cmd-3cc4bc986f4544c8, cmd-b3553e57fc4242ed). (3) A manual, non-Ansible 'ip route add' was applied directly on node2 during debugging before the equivalent route was later made persistent via the playbook (cmd-2697b61dc9b742ca) — low-risk and superseded by the final Ansible-managed state, but not itself an Ansible-driven change. (4) Manual foreground socat debugging commands were bounded and self-terminated (kill) with no residue (cmd-3503da4df68c4266, cmd-bc04b5720ae84abd). Lifecycle diffs between after-prepare and after-executor show only expected ephemeral residue (reboot.log, systemd-private tmp dirs tied to new boot IDs) with no failed services or package-manager damage on any node.
